prompt.context: Your client is the CEO of a biotechnology company, which has recently found a way to double the carbohydrates and proteins in corn using bioengineering methods. The client believes the product has commercial value. They have hired you to determine if the product has value and to whom. Additionally, it is your job to determine how much value it has.
prompt.question: Does this new bioengineered corn have commercial value? If so, to whom, and how much is it worth?

clarifying_info.q: Where are we considering producing this product and what is our geographic market?
clarifying_info.a: We are only targeting the U.S. market, which is also where production will take place. Consumer preference for corn varies by geographic location, so this is an important distinction.

clarifying_info.q: Is the only difference between our product and traditional corn the additional carbohydrates and proteins?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The additional carbohydrates and protein are the only differences between the new and old corn.
There are three categories of consumers: humans (10%), industrial production (10%), and animals (80%).
R&D costs are sunk. No money has been spent yet on commercializing the product (manufacturing, selling, etc.).

exhibits.title: Animal Feed Information (p90 reference)
exhibits.shows: A table listing nutritional content and price per bushel for old corn, new corn (price unknown), and soy, plus daily animal requirements

exhibits.title: Animal Feed Information (p92 — same table, presented at the math step)
exhibits.shows: Same animal feed nutritional and pricing table, provided when the interviewer asks the candidate to price the new corn

framework: Segment the market by customer type (humans, industrial production, animal feed) and identify value drivers for each segment
Map the product's differentiating attributes (doubled carbs and protein) against those value drivers to determine which segments benefit
Assess market size and attractiveness of targeted segments (focus on the 80% animal feed segment)
Determine pricing strategy: calculate the value the new corn delivers relative to existing alternatives (old corn + soy mix) and find the profit-maximizing price
Consider competitive dynamics, barriers to entry, and sustainability of pricing advantage

questions.prompt: Which customer segments are the best targets for the new corn, and why?
questions.guidance: Human consumption depends on vitamin/mineral content, not carbohydrate/protein content, so the new corn's extra carbs and protein add limited value for human consumers. Industrial production (starch extraction for ethanol) benefits from higher carbohydrate content. Animal feed (80% of the market) requires specific carbohydrate and protein levels and is the largest and most attractive segment. The interviewee should identify industrial and animal feed as the primary targets, with animal feed prioritized given its market size.

questions.prompt: Using the animal feed data, how would you price the new corn to push the old corn out of business (indifference pricing)?
questions.guidance: Calculate the cost of the current old-corn-plus-soy combination, then find the price at which a farmer is indifferent between the new corn alone and the old mix. The new corn should cost the same as the old corn portion of the mix (since it satisfies the carb requirement and also covers protein), adjusted by the cheapest way to meet protein needs.

math.setup: A farmer must satisfy 1000g carbs/day and 1000g protein/day. Current mix: old corn for carbs, soy for remaining protein. Old corn: 50g carbs and 25g protein per bushel at $2.50. Soy: 0g carbs and 50g protein per bushel at $3.50.
steps: Step 1 — Carb requirement with old corn: 1000g carbs / 50g per bushel = 20 bushels of old corn. Cost: 20 × $2.50 = $50/day. This also delivers 20 × 25g = 500g protein.
Step 2 — Remaining protein with soy: 1000g − 500g = 500g protein still needed. 500g / 50g per bushel = 10 bushels of soy. Cost: 10 × $3.50 = $35/day.

Step 4 — Indifference price for new corn: New corn has 100g carbs/bushel, so 1000g carbs requires 10 bushels. These 10 bushels also provide 10 × 50g = 500g protein, leaving 500g protein unmet. Farmer still needs 10 bushels of soy at $35/day. For the farmer to be indifferent, new corn cost must equal old corn cost: $50/day. At 10 bushels, price per bushel = $50 / 10 = $5.00/bushel.
Step 5 — To encourage switching, price just below $5.00 (e.g., $4.99/bushel).
math.answer: Indifference price = $5.00/bushel. Price slightly below (e.g., $4.99) to drive switching.

questions.prompt: Is the $5.00/bushel price profit-maximizing? What alternative pricing strategy could increase revenue?
questions.guidance: At $5.00/bushel the farmer buys 10 bushels of new corn ($50) plus 10 bushels of soy ($35) = $85/day total — same as before. Revenue to client = $50/day. A lower price could push soy out as well: if new corn is priced at $3.50/bushel, farmers are indifferent between new corn and soy on a protein-per-dollar basis. The farmer would use new corn alone to meet both carb and protein requirements (20 bushels × $3.50 = $70/day). Client revenue rises to $70/day, and the farmer also saves $15/day — a win-win. This strategy eliminates both old corn and soy from the farmer's mix.

math.setup: Evaluate revenue under the alternative pricing: new corn priced at $3.50/bushel, farmer uses new corn only.
steps: New corn to satisfy 1000g carbs: 1000 / 100g = 10 bushels; protein from 10 bushels = 500g. Still need 500g more protein.
New corn to satisfy remaining protein: 500g / 50g = 10 more bushels.
math.answer: Pricing at $3.50/bushel (capturing all carb+protein demand) yields $70/day revenue vs. $50/day at $5.00/bushel. $3.50 is closer to the profit-maximizing price in this scenario.

brainstorming.prompt: What other strategic considerations should the client keep in mind going forward?

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: The technology may be easily replicable; competitors will enter once they see the monopolistic opportunity
Client must invest in continued R&D to maintain a head start
Patent protection or trade secrets should be explored to extend the competitive moat

categories.name: Customer switching costs
ideas: Farmers may face switching costs (storage, testing, supply chain changes) that affect pricing strategy
Pricing should account for these costs to incentivize adoption

categories.name: Industrial production segment
ideas: The 10% industrial segment (starch extraction for ethanol) also values higher carbohydrate content
Separate pricing analysis should be done for this segment

categories.name: Market entry and scaling
ideas: Manufacturing and distribution infrastructure must be built (no commercialization spend yet)
U.S. regulatory environment for bioengineered crops could affect speed to market
Geographic variation in corn preferences could limit addressable market

categories.name: Risk management
ideas: Consumer / regulatory backlash against bioengineered crops
Dependency on single crop type; diversification of biotech applications could spread risk

recommendation: The new bioengineered corn has clear commercial value, primarily in the animal feed segment (80% of the corn market) and secondarily in industrial production (10%)

The optimal pricing strategy is approximately $3.50/bushel, which eliminates both old corn and soy from the animal feed mix, maximizes client revenue ($70/day per farmer unit vs. $50/day at indifference pricing), and delivers cost savings to farmers
risks: Technology is easily replicable; competitors will enter quickly, compressing margins
Bioengineered crop regulatory and consumer-acceptance risk could limit market penetration
Human consumption segment (10%) is unlikely to benefit due to different value drivers (vitamins/minerals vs. carbs/proteins)
next_steps: Conduct detailed analysis of the industrial production segment to determine incremental value of higher carbohydrate content
Assess R&D pipeline and patent strategy to sustain competitive advantage
Model full profitability including manufacturing, distribution, and sales costs before finalizing go-to-market pricing
Engage with regulatory bodies early to clarify bioengineered crop approval requirements
